label: context.reference
description: Create or change a trigger from a plain-language request: choose its conditions, connect its work and verify that it is armed.
text:
Use this skill when the operator asks for a reminder, scheduled work, monitoring, or an action after an event. A Trigger is the client's name for an interface with declared activation conditions, connected to ordinary runs. Choose the implementation from the request and the installed architecture; a time schedule is only one possibility.

First establish what should happen, what should cause it, where the work and result belong, and whether it repeats. Use the conversation's existing context. Ask only for a detail that changes the outcome, such as an ambiguous time, timezone, scope or recipient. Keep the operator's request as the assignment.

Read the bound architecture and authoring guidance, then inspect existing triggers and the relevant interface contracts through granted tools. Reuse or update an existing trigger when it already covers the request. Existing interfaces are examples: inspect their complete descriptor, activation, life and connected run topology. Reuse a suitable driver through its declared import. If no existing family expresses the condition, implement the needed interface inside its own authorized owner folder. Do not introduce a scheduler into the kernel.

Connect the interface to the intended existing run, or author the controller and task creation topology for separate executions. Choose the EE, worker, provider, rooms, context and result destination under their actual policy. Use independent exact interface identities where work must stay isolated; copied code grants no authority. A trigger needs an active run binding to live. Keep repeatable input routes standing and use one-shot verified waits only where evidence must close an obligation. For time conditions inspect the installed clock contract, including timezone, first firing, repeat semantics and restart behavior; do not assume cron covers every event.

Author through the available composition operations or ordinary granted file tools. Preserve unrelated configuration and protect concurrent edits. Read back the complete topology, check descriptor and policy validation, and verify activation readiness and its next due condition. An actual firing requires movement evidence; writing files alone does not prove that work ran. Do not fire a real external action merely to test it.

Tell the operator, briefly and without technical jargon, what will happen, when or under which condition, where the result will appear, and any unresolved requirement. Use terms such as trigger, task and project; explain interfaces, bindings and EEs only when asked. Never claim that a trigger is active before the installed configuration and receiving route prove it.
